entry.title: Irreal: Updating Clock Tables
entry.summary:
has an interesting problem whose solution is harder than you think it would be. The problem is pretty simple: Every Sunday morning when he writes his weekly review, he needs to update all the clock tables in his journal. That usually takes about a minute and mbork had the idea that he could use an idle timer to run the update. Specifically, he reasoned that if Emacs were idle for a minute it probably meant that he was otherwise engaged and that Emacs would be idle for another minute so why not fire off his update?
Of course, he wanted to do this only once a week on Sundays so it was a bit more complex than just setting the idle timer. He came up with the idea of setting a (normal) timer for 3 AM on Sunday that would set the idle timer. That didn’t quite work because of a technical issue but he got things working with yet another timer.
You should read his post for the details. His solution is interesting and shows that sometimes even simple things can be harder than we imagined.

entry.title: A searchable archive of everything
entry.summary:
I wrote something down recently, and later I couldn't find it. If you know me, you know why; I put my notes into too many different apps. Once in a while I declare loudly that "I'm using only this app, from now on! I mean it!" and then change my mind a month later. It's just the way I am. This most recent failure was the last straw and finally forced me to deal with it properly. Instead of fixing myself, I built a software crutch. I spent today vibe-coding an indexer and search engine for all of my stuff. Here's the initial version of a web UI:
I also hacked together a TUI and an Emacs package. Those access the data via Tailscale SSH so I don't need to worry about installing things on other machines. Just the wrapper script. Here's the list of sources being indexed (so far): ./archive index baty.net: 1272 items (0.9s) archive.baty.net: 2791 items (1.1s) linux.baty.net: 26 items (0.0s) blot.baty.net: 678 items (0.3s) jackbaty.com: 581 items (0.1s) notes: 2287 items (1.0s) dayone: 2507 items (1.4s) thebrain: 1177 items (0.5s) mail: 1 updated, 0 removed (since revision 43773) (1.6s) duplicates: 786 items in 381 groups (10.2s)
One nice thing about this is now I can search all of my Denote notes from my phone. Everything is plain files and it uses boring, durable tools, so the archive should outlive whichever apps made the content that week. Even an AI layer, if I add one, sits on top of the search instead of being built into it. The database is disposable because it only takes 10 seconds to reindex everything. Maybe now I'll be OK with all of my app churn. ✍️ Reply by email

entry.title: James Cherti: Configuring Emacs Eglot for Python with .dir-locals.el, python-lsp-server (Pylsp), and ruff
entry.summary: Setting up a Python development environment in Emacs with Eglot and python-lsp-server (pylsp) requires telling the language server which plugins to run and which ones to ignore. While you can set eglot-workspace-configuration globally, doing so forces every Python project you open using Emacs to use the same toolchain and formatting rules. Placing the configuration in a .dir-locals.el file applies these Emacs buffer settings and Eglot workspace settings to files within the project's directory tree. The indentation settings and fill-column can be chosen to match the conventions configured in pyproject.toml, while Ruff reads its own configuration from that file when applicable. … Continue reading →

entry.title: The CFP Is Expanding For The Same Reason The PCSA Is Gaining Momentum
entry.summary: ESPN is reporting that ESPN and the College Football Playoff are close to a deal to expand the playoff field to 24 teams in 2027. This news arrives merely two years after the field already expanded from four teams to 12. Not only was this expansion inevitable, but it is unlikely to be the last we see. For now, we are on the cusp of a 24-team playoff, which comes as ESPN and the CFP have been negotiating a big new deal for the network to continue broadcasting the games. According to ESPN's reporting, this new deal will do away with Power 4 conference championship games and start the season a week earlier. Details are reportedly being finalized, but ESPN describes the current composition for the 24-team field as 19 at-large bids, the Power 4 conference champions "as determined by each league," and the highest-ranked Group of 6 team. The Big Ten has been a leading proponent for this change, and its commissioner Tony Pettiti pushed back against complaints that further expansion would dilute and devalue the product and the games. He argues that the new system would include "tiered incentives." According to ESPN, seeds 1 through 8 would get a first-round bye, followed by a home game. Teams seeded from 9 through 16 would get a first-round home game, while teams seeded 17 and lower should be vying for a higher ranking, both to stay in competition and to get that first-round home game. Cool.

And so ends the Los Angeles Dodgers' reign as baseball's most overwhelming boogeyman. The poster kids for the omnipotence of money, the belief that having the best player means being the best team, the power of the big market over all it surveys—all of that feels less important at this moment than the ability to do the things the Milwaukee Brewers do better than anyone else. The same old song has been replaced, for the moment, by this:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Xzmeye6MaY
Yes, meet your new overlords. The Brewers pack extraordinary amounts of baseball into every game, play it better than anyone else, and supposedly have no interest in hitting home runs. It was fitting, then, that they gave the nation a little tweak on the cheek Thursday night en route to sweeping the Dodgers out of the postseason when the final run they scored in their 6-4 win came on a moonshot from noted Boston Red Sox ex-pat and devoted homer avoider David Hamilton. The Brewers did all the things that made them the best team in baseball this season, and mostly kept the Dodgers from doing the things that won them the last two World Series—and then they did the stuff that contemporary winning baseball teams do, too, in a typically unpredictable way.

entry.title: The Secret History Of Dodger Stadium’s Mysterious Concrete Murals
entry.summary: L.A. Material is an independent news organization aimed at filling some holes in the Los Angeles news landscape and making that fascinating, fragmented city more legible. You can learn more, and subscribe, at lamaterial.com. This story originally ran at the site on Sept. 30. I had been going to Dodger Stadium with my dad for about 30 years before he pointed them out to me. “See that?” he asked, gesturing toward two rectangular panels of concrete on a far wall of the main seating structure. They looked almost like friezes, carved with inscrutable designs. My dad had been wondering about them for decades. Turns out the pieces he’d spotted are just the beginning. Eventually I’d locate more custom bas-relief sculptures around the park—about a dozen in total. Smaller ones visible from the field-level entrances. Massive, multi-story pieces that wrap around certain outside corners of the building. They’re subtle: abstract scenes unadorned with color, camouflaged into the rest of their concrete environments, in some cases obscured by trees and bushes.

entry.title: It’s Jake Bauerses All The Way Down
entry.summary: After a flyout and a strikeout in his first two attempts, Jake Bauers's third time facing Blake Snell in Wednesday's Game 3 of the National League Championship Series went like this: Bauers took a slider down the middle of the plate for strike one. He took two non-competitive pitches down low to make the count 2-1. He foul-tipped a changeup, and then, sitting on two strikes, four pitches into his at-bat, he decided that he simply would not strike out again. So Bauers fouled off a slider in the zone, then a curveball. He laid off an inside fastball to draw the count full. Then he managed to foul off a high fastball, and, immediately after, slowed down to catch a changeup in the zone. As the pitch count for this at-bat ticked over into double digits, Bauers pulled a slider that sat up in the zone a bit too much, sending it into the stands past the right-field foul pole. On the 11th pitch, Bauers made no mistake. Snell threw a middle-middle, 98-mph fastball, and Bauers smoked a no-doubt, two-run homer that carried over 400 feet into right field to give the Milwaukee Brewers a 3-2 lead. When Bauers's teammate Garrett Mitchell hit his own home run off Snell just two pitches later, it was, comparatively, an anticlimax. Spiritually speaking, a guy hitting a home run one pitch after just missing out on another home run counts for two home runs. Bauers had already won the game; Mitchell's own homer was just overkill on Snell's way out.

entry.title: Irreal: Saving Window Configurations
entry.summary:
techhub.social, lispwizard has a short post (or whatever techhub.social calls them) on saving window configurations to registers. He notes how easy it is to save multiple configurations and switch between them on the fly.
Saving window configurations and other data in registers is an extraordinarily powerful technique that all Emacs users should learn and master. There’s a problem, though, when you want to do this programmatically: which register should you use? How can you be sure that your choice won’t conflict with a register that the user has chosen manually for some other task? There are several situations in which I want to run an Emacs function in a single window—Elfeed is an example—and I do that by saving the current window configuration, deleting the other windows, running the required function, and then restoring the previous window configuration but how do I choose a “safe” register to save the window configuration in?
The answer is a trick I learned from Magnar Sveen years ago. Instead of using a letter to name the register, you use a symbol like :saved-windows. That works because when you name a register with a letter, Emacs uses a pointer to its symbol as the register name. Using a symbol name like :saved-windows works because the result is also a symbol pointer.
If you have the need to save something in a register programmatically, this is a good way of doing it. You don’t have to worry about conflicts because the user can not use symbol names for registers interactively.

entry.title: Irreal: Org-ibullets
entry.summary:
a simple package that trades Org mode’s heading stars for UTF-8 bullets. If you’re like me, your first thought is, “Doesn’t that already exist?” Sort of. What already exists is the no longer maintained org-bullets. Cherti’s package is called org-ibullets (note the i).
Cherti explains the differences from org-bullets in his announcement. The TL;DR is that he’s optimized org-ibullets by eliminating redundant computations, eliminated spurious syntax warnings that org-bullets could produce, and made some improvements at the source level.
As I said, the package is simple. It can be used right out of the box but you can customize the list of bullets and their face if you desire. This seems like a very nice package if you’d like to make your Org buffers look a little nicer.

entry.title: Meta Redux: neorepl: A Terminal REPL for Clojure (and Friends)
entry.summary: For more than a decade the Clojure REPL most people saw in a terminal was REPLy, the one behind lein repl. It served us well, but it’s showing its age, and I kept wishing for a terminal REPL that felt like CIDER, without the Emacs part. So I finally built one. neorepl 0.1 is out today! Why another REPL? There’s no shortage of Clojure REPLs, so it’s fair to ask. Here’s what I was after: nREPL all the way down. neorepl only speaks nREPL, so it works with anything that runs an nREPL server: Clojure, babashka, shadow-cljs, Basilisp, ClojureCLR and so on. The smarts live on the server. When cider-nrepl is there neorepl uses it, the same way CIDER does, and when it isn’t it falls back to nREPL’s built-in ops, and then to evaluating a bit of code. A REPL that’s pleasant to use: a proper line edit…

entry.title: Irreal: Still More On Entering Ranges
entry.summary:
quick post on Sacha’s solution to a problem posed by David Pape. I thought it was a nice solution but then 0-_-0_ pointed out that abo-abo had already solved this problem with his tiny library. So I wrote about that and prepared to move on.
I was not allowed to. Frequent commenter Phil remarked in my original post that he would use a keyboard macro. He suggested that that would make sense for those of us who who seldom need to enter a sequence of ranges like Pape. In Pape’s case this was something that he needed to do a lot so a solution like Sacha’s or abo-abo’s make sense. I agree with Phil. A keyboard macro is exactly how I would solve this problem given that I seldom have it.
This seems pretty obvious and might not be worth writing about except that Phil’s solution showed me something that I didn’t know: You can set the initial value of the counter with a Ctrl+u n where n is the desired initial value. That’s a lot easier than using Ctrl+x Ctrl+k Ctrl+c to do the job.
As a final note, I think that Phil had a typo in his macro. As far as I can tell it should be
C-u 47 <f3> # <f3> , SPC <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4>
At least that’s what works for me.
It turns out that I regularly use a macro with a counter so I’m really happy to learn that the counter can be set so easily.
Update [2026-10-10 Sat 12:12]: Fixed link.
